summary: The note describes a growing shift in schools toward nature-based and outdoor learning, as of autumn 2023. It surveys international models (Sweden, Japan, Māori, Singapore) and US and Canadian examples of outdoor classrooms, agricultural education, tech-enabled outdoor study, and wellbeing programs. It also notes challenges such as funding, teacher training and standardized tests, and argues they can be overcome through creativity and community involvement.
one_line: Schools worldwide are adopting nature-based learning, with examples from several countries and US schools, psychosocial benefits, and challenges like funding and testing.
key_facts: Sweden regularly uses forests as natural classrooms for preschools and schools, as part of outdoor pedagogy.
In Japan, Shinrin-yoku (forest bathing) has moved from a national health practice into an educational experience for children.
The Māori concept of 'Kaitiakitanga' in New Zealand fosters guardianship of the environment and has been integrated into certain curricula to teach sustainability.
Singapore, called the "City in a Garden," is developing curricula that include urban farming and biodiversity studies.

On September 15, 2023, Riverdale Elementary School in California held a ribbon-cutting for a new outdoor classroom with native plants, a fruit orchard and a vegetable garden, championed by Principal Linda Brown.
On October 3, 2023, Alfonso Reyes of Mountain View High School in Colorado began a year-long student project monitoring local water quality and its effects on community health.

The Agri-Cultural program, started in October 2023 at Harvest Secondary School in rural Nebraska by Sarah Thompson, has students manage a small farm plot covering crop rotation, soil science and farm economics.
On September 28, 2023, Fremont Middle School in Oregon launched a pilot where students used tablets and apps to document species diversity, guided by teacher Mark Lee.
Toronto is implementing mandatory weekly outdoor classes called 'Nature Nurture Time' for all elementary schools starting November 2023, overseen by child psychologist Dr. Emily Sanders.
Studies cited say learning in natural environments can reduce stress, improve mood, increase attention capacity and bolster self-discipline.
Key challenges are funding for outdoor classrooms, teacher training, and adjusting curricula to standardized test requirements.
Acorn Academy in Tennessee revamped its curriculum for environmental education with minimal budget impact using grant writing, local fundraising and partnerships with environmental organizations.
